extracted.intended_audience: writers of English prose; readers of The Spectator; essayists and general readers interested in style and moral writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for English prose and essay writing: emphasis on brevity, clarity, national genius of language, moral effect on readers, truthful narration, and avoidance of pedantry or useless circumstantiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The English language is 'wonderfully adapted to a Man ... sparing of his Words, and an Enemy to Loquacity.' Prose should be delivered 'in the shortest way we are able' so that thought is given quick birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise phrasing and compact arrangement of matter; clump ideas closely rather than sprawling; prefer short sounds (monosyllables) where they express ideas readily. Example observations: English abounds in monosyllables which let us deliver thoughts in few sounds; the matter of our writings lies in a 'narrower Compass' than foreign authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of monosyllables and rapid pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Monosyllables give opportunity to deliver thoughts in few sounds and make ideas readiest; many multi-syllable words of Latin derivation are contracted in speech to suit English rapidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monosyllables and compressed pronunciation to match the natural genius of English prose when clarity and dispatch of thought are desired. Examples: words like 'Liberty, Conspiracy, Theatre, Orator' are often pronounced more compactly in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harmful over-abbreviation and truncation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent changes—abbreviating past-tense terminations (drown'd, walk'd), substituting -s for -eth (drowns, walks), and other pruning—have 'disfigured the Tongue' and created clusters of consonants and a hissing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While speech abridges words, preserve necessary vowels and endings in writing and in solemn contexts to protect elegance and etymology. Be cautious about pruning spelling to match pronunciation; excessive truncation damages the language's grace and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive colloquial contractions and informal abbreviations in serious writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractions and clipped forms (mayn't, can't, shd'n't, wo'n't) and abbreviations (mob., rep., pos., incog.) may suit familiar speech but risk coarsening or confusing written prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve colloquial contractions and shorthand for appropriate informal contexts; do not let them unduly encroach on more formal or permanent writing where they may become inelegant or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language should reflect the national genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiarities of a language flow from the genius and temper of its people: English terseness mirrors English modesty and thoughtfulness; French talkativeness appears in their tongue; Italian musicality shapes their phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose tone, cadence, and diction that suit the cultural/psychological character you wish to convey; align language features with the temperament of the people or characters represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and mixture of useful and delightful notions
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful periodical or essayist supplies a 'Variety of subjects' that 'freight[s] either with useful or delightful Notions'—each paragraph giving either improvement or entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose work to both inform and delight: alternate or combine instructive content with pleasurable expression; avoid being purely didactic or purely frivolous. The Spectator's effect is praised for making 'a deeper Impression' and affecting 'the secret Springs of the Mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral persuasion that pleases rather than preaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective moral writing 'charms the Fancy, sooth[s] the Passions, and insensibly lead[s] the Reader to that Sweetness of Temper that you so well describe; you rouse Generosity ... and inculcate Humanity with that Ease.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming to reform or instruct, use gentle, engaging rhetoric rather than blunt condemnation; aim to 'please and instruct' so readers are moved toward virtue without feeling shamed. The Spectator is lauded as offering an 'infallible Cure of Vice and Folly' by subtle means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless circumstantiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive insistence on minutiae—overly setting geography, parentage, collateral alliances, or trivial particulars—wastes the reader's time and distracts from the main point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include particulars that serve the central effect or argument; omit extraneous exactness or prolix detailing that does not advance the narrative or point. The essays critique 'ordinary Story-tellers' who are 'careful to be exact' in unimportant particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry and knotty exposition of clear matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not turn clear cases into unnecessarily 'learned and knotty' expositions or raise frivolous doubts; refrain from proving what no one denies or complicating plain truths with needless authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clarity and plain reasoning rather than showing erudition for its own sake. The text ridicules those who 'labour to raise Arguments with you about Matters you will give up to them without the least Controversy' or who 'put you to prove that Snow is white.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and restraint in imaginative narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Imaginative embellishment that amounts to habitual falsehood ('one of the greatest Liars') may entertain but risks deceiving, creating scandal, or making others objects of ridicule. The 'Historian' in conversation 'cannot be contented with ordinary Occurrences' and invents particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use invention with care: avoid fabrications that defame or expose acquaintances to ridicule; do not let fancy override responsibility. If employing fictionalized or exaggerated anecdotes, ensure they do not harm real people or undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy and seeing from other conditions (character portrayal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer or master should 'put themselves in the Condition of the Persons below them' to understand commands and preserve humane behaviour; such sympathy produces more harmonious households and truer depiction of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying social relations or writing characters, adopt the perspective of those of different ranks or conditions; let empathy inform behavior, motive, and dialogue so characters ring true and humane. Example: Pamphilio's household is happy because he 'place[s] himself in their Condition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Let actions reveal character (show, don't merely assert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good representation arises from showing humane regard and daily behavior rather than abstract claims; small actions (apologies, understanding circumstances) illustrate a person's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate virtues and faults through concrete gestures and incidents in the narrative, as when a master apologises for attendants or preserves equanimity—these details convey character more effectively than general statements.
